value.overview: The Chestnut-capped Brushfinch is a medium-sized New World sparrow of humid mountain forests in Central and South America. It is named for its rich chestnut crown, which contrasts with a dark face, olive-brown upperparts, and pale underparts. Usually encountered alone or in pairs, it spends much of its time in dense understory and leaf litter, where it searches for insects, seeds, and other small food items.
value.classification: The Chestnut-capped Brushfinch belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows, and the genus Arremon. Several geographic forms are recognized across its broad, discontinuous range.
value.identification: Adults are about 18–19 cm long. The most distinctive features are the chestnut-colored crown and nape, dark markings around the face and sides of the head, an olive-brown back, and a pale throat and breast with darker streaking or shading across the upper breast. The bill is short and conical, suited to seed eating, while the rounded body and relatively short tail reflect its mainly terrestrial lifestyle. Its quiet, skulking habits can make it easier to hear than see.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Mexico through Central America and the Andes to Peru and Venezuela. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the mountain ranges, including humid and wet subtropical forest, cloud forest, and mature secondary woodland, generally from about 900 to 2,000 meters elevation. It favors dense understory, tangles, bamboo or other low vegetation, forest edges, and areas with substantial leaf litter. It is recorded in suitable highland habitats across several parts of the country.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally nonmigratory throughout its range. Individuals may make local movements in response to elevation, weather, or food availability, but it is not a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in humid upland forest and other dense habitats within the species’ range. The nest is built in secluded vegetation near the ground or at low height, where it is concealed among roots, banks, dense plants, or other cover. As with many forest brushfinches, both adults are believed to contribute to territorial defense and care of the young. Detailed breeding information is uneven across the range, and timing varies geographically; Costa Rican birds are resident rather than seasonal migrants.
value.dietFeeding: The Chestnut-capped Brushfinch feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, seeds, and some small fruits. It forages mostly on the ground or in low vegetation, using its bill to turn over leaves and probe among debris. It may occasionally attend army-ant swarms, taking prey disturbed by the ants, but it usually forages alone or in pairs and only rarely joins mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.behavior: This brushfinch is a secretive, ground-oriented bird that moves through dense understory with quick hops and short runs. While feeding, it may raise the crown feathers and fluff the throat feathers, producing a distinctive alert appearance. It is usually detected singly or in pairs and tends to remain close to cover. Its song and calls help reveal its presence in forested mountain habitats, although the species can be difficult to observe clearly.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species is not currently considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline for a threatened category.
